# Education in Nigeria: Overview and Structure
Education in Nigeria is structured into three main levels: primary, secondary, and tertiary, with additional provisions for vocational, informal, and adult literacy programs. Primary education typically starts at age 5, lasts six years, and encompasses core subjects such as Mathematics, English, religious knowledge, and one indigenous language (Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, or Igbo), with private schools offering additional subjects like Computer Science and French. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program, established in 1999, guarantees free, compulsory, and uninterrupted nine-year formal schooling (6 years of primary plus 3 years of junior secondary), monitored by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC). Secondary education comprises six years split into three years each of Junior and Senior Secondary School, with a curriculum including compulsory and elective subjects, and technical colleges available for trade-oriented education. Admission to federal and state secondary schools is merit-based, often through the Common Entrance Examination; private schools charge considerably higher fees and generally provide better facilities.
Tertiary education in Nigeria includes universities, polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education, administered by both government and private sectors. Admission requires passing the West African Examination Council (WAEC) or National Examination Council (NECO) senior secondary exams, plus the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) test. Nigeria currently hosts over 153 registered universities, with ongoing expansion of private universities. Vocational and technical education is administered by the National Board for Technical Education, offering both formal certificates and apprenticeships. Literacy rates remain a challenge, particularly in northern regions; the adult literacy rate was 69% in 2022, with ongoing government initiatives targeting improvement in both traditional and digital literacy. There are special programs focusing on marginalized groups and increased support for female education, though barriers persist due to poverty, cultural factors, and conflict. International schools, A-level programs (IJMB, JUPEB), and informal literacy efforts contribute further to educational diversity and access.
